newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Hamas warns Washington, Israel against extradition.
newsitem.headline: Hamas warns Washington, Israel against extradition.

text.p: The militant Hamas movement in Gaza warned the United States on Wednesday that if it extradites to Israel a leader of the Islamic group's political arm, America would become an enemy of "Islamic people everywhere."

Lawyers for jailed Hamas leader Mousa Mohammed Abu Marzook said in New York on Friday he had decided to abandon his legal challenge to the extradition. Abu Marzook can be sent back to Israel within about 60 days.
Hamas spokesman Mahmoud al-Zahar told a news conference in Gaza City the extradition, if carried out, could threaten the fragile calm in the "whole Islamic area."
"We warn the USA that it will bear the whole responsibility of the status of unrest which will emerge as a result of handing Dr Marzook to Israel," Zahar said.
The extradition "would place America as an enemy of Islamic people everywhere, because kidnapping Mousa Abu Marzook and sending him to Israel is an act against all Moslems," he said.

Israel announced in 1995 that it had formally asked the United States to hand over Abu Marzook, who was arrested in July of that year at a New York airport as he flew to the United States, where he had lived for at least 15 years.
Israel alleged he was responsible, as head of Hamas' political arm, for attacks that killed scores of Israelis. It did not contend that he had personally carried out violent acts.
"We also warn the Israeli Likud government of delivering Dr Marzook at a time that all the Palestinian people are looking for freeing all prisoners," Zahar said.
Though Israel has released thousands of jailed Palestinians since signing a landmark accord with Yasser Arafat's PLO in 1993, thousands more remain in the Jewish state's prisons.
Zahar did not detail the nature of a possible Hamas response to the extradition. However, he said, "We cannot guarantee that no one will do something against Americans."
Abu Marzook's lawyers said he abandoned his appeal despite their feeling that they had a strong case.
They said their client had lost faith in the U.S. justice system after being imprisoned for 18 months without being charged with a crime.

Abu Marzook argued he had been involved only in political matters, which are not extraditable offences. But a U.S. district judge ordered his extradition last May, saying he was involved in an "agreement to accomplish an unlawful act."

The judge refused to allow a hearing on Abu Marzook's argument that the offences charged by Israel were not covered by the treaty with the United States because of the political offence exception. Abu Marzook's lawyers said this denial was unprecedented but it was upheld by another judge in October.
